BANGALORE, India (CNN) -- Two-year-old Lakshmi Tatma, an Indian toddler born with four arms and four legs, made her first public appearance Tuesday, a week after surgeons in India successfully removed her additional limbs. Doctors said Lakshmi was recovering well as she appeared Tuesday at a news conference. Lakshmi, wearing a plaster cast on her legs to keep her feet up and her legs together to help her wounds heal, was carried into a news conference Tuesday as her doctors announced she was being released from intensive care. "She is coping very well," lead surgeon Dr. Sharan Patil said. "She is being carried around by her mother and her father." Several of her doctors, all of them smiling, described her recovery over the past week "very steady and good progress," one saying she is "out of the woods" as far as serious medical issues are concerned.  Watch the recovering little girl meet the media » . The operation a week ago lasted 27 hours and involved a team of some 30 surgeons, all specialists in pediatrics, neurosurgery, orthopedics, and plastic surgery, working in eight-hour shifts. Lakshmi's extra limbs were part of a conjoined twin which stopped developing in the womb. It had a torso and limbs but no head, and was joined to Lakshmi at the pelvis. Doctors said that without the surgery, Lakshmi would have been unlikely to survive beyond early adolescence. The surgery involved the removal of the extra limbs and the repositioning of Lakshmi's organs. When Lakshmi was born into her poor, rural Indian family, villagers in the remote settlement of Rampur Kodar Katti in the northern state of Bihar believed she was sacred. As news of her birth spread, locals queued for a blessing from the baby. Her parents, Shambhu and Poonam Tatma, named the girl after the Hindu goddess of wealth who has four arms. However, they were forced to keep her in hiding after they were approached by men offering money in exchange for putting their daughter in a circus. The couple, who earn just $1 a day as casual laborers, wanted her to have the operation but were unable to pay for the rare procedure, which had never before been performed in India. After Patil visited the girl in her village from Narayana Health City hospital in Bangalore, the hospital's foundation agreed to fund the $200,000 operation. Planning for the surgery took a month, Patil said, and Lakshmi spent that month in the hospital. Many villagers, however, remained opposed to surgery and were planning to erect a temple to Lakshmi, whom they still revere as sacred. E-mail to a friend .

Lakshmi Tatma, a two-year-old toddler from a rural village in India, captured international attention when she made her first public appearance just one week after undergoing a groundbreaking surgical procedure to remove her extra limbs. Born with four arms and four legs, Lakshmi's condition stemmed from a rare medical phenomenon that had made her the subject of both fascination and concern within her community and among medical professionals worldwide.

## The Surgical Procedure

The operation to separate Lakshmi from her extra limbs was an extraordinarily complex undertaking, spanning approximately 27 hours in total. A dedicated team of around 30 specialist surgeons collaborated on the procedure, working in carefully coordinated shifts to manage the physical and mental demands of such a lengthy and delicate operation. The additional limbs, doctors explained, belonged to a conjoined twin that had ceased developing properly in the womb, leaving Lakshmi with the extraordinary but medically dangerous condition of having four arms and four legs fused to her body.

## Recovery and Prognosis

In the days following the surgery, medical staff reported encouraging news about Lakshmi's condition. Her recovery was described as "very steady," and doctors confirmed that she had successfully moved out of intensive care, having passed through the most critical and high-risk phase of post-operative recovery. This progress was seen as a significant milestone, given the complexity and duration of the surgery she had endured.

Medical experts emphasized the critical nature of the intervention, noting that without the surgery, Lakshmi's chances of survival into her teenage years would have been slim. The extra limbs posed serious ongoing health risks and complications that, left unaddressed, were expected to become increasingly life-threatening as she grew older. The surgery, therefore, was not merely a matter of physical normalization but a life-saving necessity.

## Cultural Significance and Challenges

Lakshmi's condition carried profound cultural weight within her rural community. Her physical resemblance to the Hindu goddess Lakshmi—who is traditionally depicted with multiple arms—led many in her village to regard her as a sacred or divine figure. This religious reverence, however, brought unforeseen complications for her family. As word of her condition spread, they found themselves needing to shield Lakshmi from individuals seeking to exploit her unique appearance for financial gain, forcing them to hide her away rather than allow her to be treated as a spectacle or source of profit.

Lakshmi Tatma, a two-year-old girl from a small village in the Indian state of Bihar, has made a remarkable public appearance just one week after undergoing a marathon 27-hour surgery to separate her from a parasitic conjoined twin, giving her a chance at a normal life for the first time.

Lakshmi was born with four arms and four legs, the result of a rare condition in which her twin stopped developing early in the womb but remained attached to her body, its limbs and pelvis fused to her own. The additional limbs, though not functional, made it nearly impossible for Lakshmi to sit, stand, or move without significant difficulty. Her parents, who come from a poor farming family, had struggled for years to understand her condition and find medical help, with many in their community regarding her as a manifestation of a Hindu goddess due to her multiple limbs—a belief that brought her a strange mixture of reverence and isolation.

A team of approximately 30 specialists—including surgeons, anesthesiologists, and support staff—worked together in a painstaking operation that lasted 27 hours. The surgery involved carefully separating the conjoined twin's remaining limbs and underdeveloped body parts from Lakshmi's own, while also repositioning her internal organs, which had been compressed and displaced due to the extra mass attached to her torso.

The procedure carried enormous risk. Doctors had warned that without intervention, Lakshmi's body would likely not have been able to sustain the strain of the extra limbs and organs as she grew older, and it was widely believed she would not have survived beyond early adolescence. The surgery, therefore, was not simply about improving her quality of life—it was considered essential to saving it.

Following the operation, Lakshmi spent several days in intensive care, closely monitored by medical staff as her body began the delicate process of healing and adjusting to its new configuration. Given the scale of the surgery, doctors had cautioned that recovery would be slow and that complications could still arise in the days and weeks following the procedure.

Remarkably, just seven days after the surgery, Lakshmi was well enough to be presented publicly, offering the first visual confirmation of the operation's success. Photographs and footage showed her in a stable condition, a significant milestone that reassured both her family and the medical team that the most dangerous phase of her recovery had passed.

The case drew international attention, both for the rarity of Lakshmi's condition and for the extraordinary medical effort required to treat her. Doctors expressed cautious optimism about her long-term prognosis, noting that while she would require further monitoring, therapy, and possibly additional procedures as she grew, the successful separation surgery represented the critical first step toward giving her a chance at a normal childhood.

For Lakshmi's family, the outcome marked the end of a long and uncertain journey, and the beginning of a new chapter in which their daughter could, for the first time, look forward to a future unburdened by the medical condition that had defined her earliest years of life.

**BANGALORE, India (CNN)** — Nestled in the southern state of Karnataka, Bangalore has earned its reputation as India's technology capital, often referred to as the "Silicon Valley of India." Over the past three decades, this bustling metropolis has transformed from a quiet garden city into a global hub for information technology, software development, and innovation.

## A Tech Powerhouse

The city hosts headquarters and major offices for numerous multinational corporations, including Infosys, Wipro, and various international tech giants who have established significant operations here. Bangalore's tech parks buzz with activity as thousands of engineers, developers, and entrepreneurs work on cutting-edge projects that serve clients around the world.

## Economic Impact

Bangalore contributes significantly to India's GDP and has played a crucial role in positioning the country as a major player in the global IT services industry. The city's success has attracted talent from across India and abroad, leading to a diverse, cosmopolitan population that blends traditional Indian culture with modern, global influences.

## Challenges of Rapid Growth

However, this rapid expansion hasn't come without challenges. Bangalore grapples with:

- **Traffic congestion** that has become notorious among residents
- **Infrastructure strain** as the population continues to grow
- **Water scarcity** issues affecting both residents and businesses
- **Environmental concerns** related to urbanization

## Looking Forward

Despite these challenges, Bangalore continues to attract investment and talent, cementing its status as a critical node in the global technology ecosystem. The city's universities and research institutions continue to produce skilled graduates, while its startup ecosystem thrives with innovative companies tackling everything from artificial intelligence to biotechnology.

As India continues its economic ascent on the world stage, Bangalore remains at the forefront—a symbol of the country's technological ambitions and a testament to how a city can reinvent itself in the digital age.

**NEW DELHI** — A two-year-old girl from a small village in the eastern Indian state of Bihar has undergone a complex, high-risk surgery to remove four extra limbs, a condition caused by a rare disorder in which a partially formed conjoined twin was absorbed into her body during pregnancy.

Lakshmi Tatma was born with a total of eight limbs — four arms and four legs — attached to her torso at the pelvis. Doctors say the additional limbs belonged to an unformed conjoined twin that failed to fully separate in the womb, a condition known as ischiopagus. The extra limbs had no matching head, and the second set of organs, including a kidney, were also fused to Lakshmi's body.

In her home village, some residents reportedly viewed Lakshmi as a reincarnation of the Hindu goddess Lakshmi, who is often depicted with four arms. Others saw her condition as a curse, contributing to the family's isolation and financial hardship.

Lakshmi's parents, Shambu and Poonam Tatma, both laborers earning just a few dollars a day, said they had no way to pay for the surgery their daughter needed to survive and eventually walk. Doctors had warned that without the operation, the strain on her heart, kidneys, and spine from supporting the extra limbs could prove fatal within a few years.

A team of more than 30 surgeons at Sparsh Hospital in Bangalore performed the marathon procedure, which lasted about 27 hours over multiple stages. The operation, led by pediatric surgeon Dr. Sharan Patil, involved carefully separating the extra limbs, reconstructing Lakshmi's pelvis, repairing her spine, and rebuilding internal organs that had been distorted by the extra mass attached to her body.

"This was one of the most complex surgeries we have ever undertaken," Dr. Patil said following the procedure. "The risk of infection, blood loss, and organ failure was extremely high, but the team worked meticulously to give this child a chance at a normal life."

Doctors said Lakshmi remained in intensive care following the surgery as she recovered from the trauma of the operation, but early signs were encouraging. Physicians said that with extensive physical therapy, she may eventually be able to walk on her own.

The case drew international attention, with donations and offers of medical assistance arriving from around the world after images of Lakshmi's condition were published by media outlets. The hospital said it would cover the bulk of the surgical costs, easing the burden on her family.

Rare conditions like Lakshmi's occur in an estimated one in a million births worldwide, though experts note that many cases go undocumented in areas with limited access to prenatal care and diagnostic imaging.

For Lakshmi's parents, the surgery represented not just a medical milestone but the hope of a childhood free from the stigma and physical burden that had defined her short life so far.

"We just want her to live like other children," her father said. "To run, to play, to go to school one day."

# The Girl They Called Divine: A Bihar Village Reckons with Faith and Reality

**MADHUBANI DISTRICT, Bihar** — In the small village of Rampur Diha, nestled among mustard fields in this northern Bihar district, the birth of Kalyani three years ago sent ripples of astonishment through the community. Born with a rare congenital condition that gave her skin an unusual golden-yellow pigmentation and eyes that seemed to shimmer amber in sunlight, the infant was quickly proclaimed by elders to be an incarnation of Goddess Lakshmi herself.

"When the midwife brought her out, there was complete silence in the room," recalls her grandmother, Sushila Devi, sitting on a charpoy outside the family's modest brick home. "Then someone whispered 'Lakshmi Mata has come to us,' and within hours, the whole village knew."

## From Miracle to Ritual

For months, Kalyani's family home became an impromptu shrine. Villagers arrived with marigold garlands, coins, and small offerings of rice and turmeric, seeking blessings from the child they believed embodied divine prosperity. Her parents, daily wage laborers with modest means, found themselves suddenly at the center of a spiritual phenomenon they neither sought nor fully understood.

"We didn't know what to think," says her father, Ramesh Manjhi, wiping sweat from his brow after a day working in the fields. "People touched her feet. They asked her to bless their harvests, their marriages. What do you say to that when she's just your daughter?"

Local priest Pandit Shivkumar Jha initially encouraged the devotion, citing ancient texts describing divine manifestations in human form. Special pujas were conducted. Word spread to neighboring villages, and for a time, Rampur Diha saw an unusual influx of visitors.

## Medical Reality Meets Tradition

The turning point came when a visiting health worker from a government medical camp examined Kalyani and gently suggested the family consult a specialist in Patna. Doctors there diagnosed her with a rare skin pigmentation disorder, unrelated to any supernatural cause but requiring monitoring for potential complications.

"These conditions, while uncommon, have straightforward medical explanations," said Dr. Anita Kumari, a pediatrician who later treated Kalyani. "Unfortunately, in areas with limited health literacy, such children can be mistaken for something otherworldly—sometimes celebrated, sometimes tragically, feared or ostracized."

The diagnosis created quiet tension within the village. Some elders quietly stepped back from their earlier proclamations, embarrassed. Others insisted the medical explanation didn't diminish the child's special nature—perhaps, they reasoned, the goddess had simply chosen a scientifically explicable vessel.

## Living Between Two Worlds

Today, Kalyani is a curious, giggling three-year-old who enjoys chasing chickens in the courtyard and has little awareness of the reverence and controversy her birth once inspired. The offerings have slowed to a trickle, mostly from a few devoted elderly women who still visit on auspicious days.

Her mother, Kamla Devi, expresses mixed feelings about those early months. "Some days it was frightening, all those strangers wanting to touch her, hold her. But I won't lie—we were also very poor, and people were generous during that time. It helped us survive."

The family has since used the goodwill and modest donations to send Kalyani's older brother to a better school in the district town. Ramesh has taken on additional work, in part because he no longer wishes to depend on his daughter's perceived divinity for the family's needs.

## A Village's Evolving Understanding

Sunita Kumari, a schoolteacher in Rampur Diha, believes the episode reflects broader tensions in rural Bihar between deep-rooted faith and expanding access to modern medicine and education.

"Our people are not foolish," she says firmly. "When something extraordinary happens and you have no other explanation, you turn to what you know—your gods, your stories. But when knowledge comes, most people are willing to adjust their understanding. It doesn't mean they stop believing in the divine. It just changes how they see this particular child."

Pandit Jha, now more measured in his position, offers a similar reflection. "Perhaps she is not literally Lakshmi Mata. # Indian Toddler Born With Eight Limbs Undergoes Life-Changing Surgery

*A remarkable medical story that captured global attention echoes similar cases from India's past*

When a child is born with multiple limbs in parts of rural India, the birth often carries a complex weight—part medical emergency, part spiritual event. This pattern has repeated itself in India's healthcare system, most famously in the widely reported case of Deepak Kumar Paswan, an Indian boy born in 2006 with extra limbs attached to his torso, a condition that led some villagers to view him as a reincarnation of the Hindu deity Vishnu, often depicted with four arms.

## The Medical Reality: Parasitic Twin Syndrome

Cases like this are typically diagnosed as **ischiopagus tripus** or a related condition involving a "parasitic twin"—a rare phenomenon where a partially formed twin fails to fully separate in early pregnancy and remains attached to the surviving, developed twin. The dependent twin often lacks a functioning brain and heart, surviving only through blood supply shared with its sibling.

Dr. Sharan Patil, the surgeon who led the widely publicized operation on Paswan at Bangalore's Sparsh Hospital, described the case as one of the most complex he had encountered, given the extensive network of shared blood vessels, bone structures, and soft tissue connecting the extra limbs to the child's pelvis and abdomen.

### The Procedure

The surgery to remove parasitic limbs is high-risk and highly specialized, generally requiring:

- **A multidisciplinary surgical team** — typically including pediatric surgeons, orthopedic specialists, vascular surgeons, and anesthesiologists
- **Extensive pre-operative imaging** — CT scans and MRIs to map shared blood vessels and skeletal attachments
- **A lengthy operation** — Paswan's surgery reportedly lasted around 27 hours, split across multiple sessions
- **Careful reconstruction** — surgeons often need to rebuild pelvic structures and reroute blood vessels once the extra limbs are removed

## The Cost Question

For families in rural India, the financial burden of such surgery would ordinarily be insurmountable. In Paswan's case and similar ones, hospitals and charitable organizations have historically stepped in to cover costs entirely, recognizing both the medical significance and the family's inability to pay. Estimates for such complex reconstructive surgeries in Indian private hospitals have ranged well into the **tens of thousands of dollars**, a sum far beyond the reach of most families in the region, where annual incomes can amount to a small fraction of that figure.

## Cultural and Religious Dimensions

What makes these cases especially notable is the intersection of modern medicine with deep-rooted religious belief. In Hindu tradition, multiple limbs are strongly associated with divinity—gods such as Vishnu, Shiva, and Durga are commonly depicted with four or more arms, symbolizing extraordinary power and cosmic responsibility.

As a result, families and communities have sometimes been reluctant to pursue surgery, viewing the child's condition as sacred rather than pathological. Paswan reportedly was worshipped by visitors before his surgery, with some traveling considerable distances to see him. Convincing families to proceed with potentially life-saving operations has occasionally required careful, culturally sensitive conversations between doctors and relatives, balancing respect for belief with urgent medical necessity, since these conditions—if untreated—often pose serious health risks including spinal complications, mobility issues, and organ strain.

## Life After Surgery

Following successful separation surgeries, children have generally been reported to recover well, eventually regaining normal mobility and continuing ordinary childhoods—a dramatic transformation from lives that otherwise would have been defined by extraordinary physical limitation.
